t: Why Your Time-Out May Be A Waste Of Time
q: The thinking is that a student in time-out will miss too much participation time. They’ll grow bored and antsy and start misbehaving.
But this progression of thought doesn’t happen in five minutes. Or even 10 minutes. Your students need every bit of 15 minutes to take ownership of their mistakes.
When you enforce consequences calmly, consistently, and without causing friction, the process of reflection and responsibility comes naturally.
This is why it’s so important that time-out be as impersonal and consistent as a metronome. You’re a robot following orders, nothing more.
But length of time isn’t the problem. Students play around in time-out when they feel the consequence is unfair.
Make time-out matter to your students. Heap the responsibility for being there entirely upon their shoulders. Give them 15 minutes to stew and reflect and own up to their wrongdoing.

t: Are You Praising Too Much To Start The School Year? ool-year/
q: That is, we recommend praise based on exceptional effort or new (but challenging) learning.
So you go overboard. You praise too often. You praise too enthusiastically. You praise for things that, frankly, aren’t worthy of it.
When you stray outside the guidelines of effective, meaningful praise, you send the message that the common, the everyday, and the expected is worthy of special recognition.
When you jump out of your shoes to give praise for what your students have already proven they can do, or for average or expected work, you render praise for true accomplishment less meaningful.
Teachers who praise often, loud, and carelessly struggle with listening and respect because they prove themselves early on to be disingenuous.
Commit yourself to praising only new and challenging learning. Praise effort that goes beyond what your class or an individual student has done before.

t: How A First-Day-Of-School Lesson Can Improve Classroom Management For The Rest Of The Year ve-classroom-management-for-the-rest-of-the-year/
q: You see, one of the best things you can do on the first day of school is set the bar of what is normal far above what your students are used to.
Furthermore, on the first day of school your students will be more open to change than at any other time during the year.

The way the strategy works is that you’re going to teach your students a common, everyday routine—like how to enter the classroom in the morning—in a way that is highly, minutely, even obsessively, detailed.
Borrow a student’s backpack and, while pretending to be an actual member of your class, perform the morning routine precisely how you want your students to do it.
Resist the urge to talk them through the routine—which will weaken rather than strengthen performance and create dependency on you.
When they finish, if they get it right, be sure and tell them that it’s perfect, that it can’t be done any better. Many teachers are afraid to do this.

t: How To Build Rapport On The First Day Of School https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2015/08/08/how-to-build-rapport-on-the-first-day-of-school/
q: Stand at your classroom door and personally say hello to every student as they walk in. Look them in the eye, ask them their name, and then introduce yourself.
The oft-recommended advice that you should never smile the first month of the school year is hogwash. In fact, smiling generously on the very first day is a great way to build rapport.
It’s important on the first day of school for your students to see you as a real person, and not a robot built by the government to tell them what to do.
Promise that you will never yell or speak to them disrespectfully. It’s a simple statement, but so, so powerful—for both them and you.
They create leverage and influence, instant likability and leadership presence. They make your immovable boundary lines of behavior matter to students.
Your students will exit your classroom excited to tell their parents how much they love their new teacher and can’t wait to get to school the next day.

t: 3 Big Mistakes Teachers Make When Enforcing Consequences ing-consequences/
q: Sighing, glaring, frowning, and the like create friction and animosity, which takes the focus off the student and their misbehavior and makes it a personal feud between you.
Another common mistake is to enforce a consequence and then wait for a response. Most teachers do this because they want the student to verbally answer for their misbehavior.
It provides an opening for the student to justify for their misbehavior, point the finger elsewhere, or try to convince you that you didn’t see what you just saw.

Instead of allowing the consequence to work, the teacher will express their disappointment in the student. They’ll tell them how they should feel, what they should think, and how they should behave the next time.
When a student misbehaves, your only job is to inform. It’s to hold accountable in the least disruptive way so your classroom management plan can do its good work.
This way, you safeguard your relationship with the student. You allow them to ponder their mistake and take responsibility for it.
